quote.translation: Kant further argued, on the ground that "only the mathematician can determine the ratio of insufficient Grounds to sufficient Grounds" (ibid.), that the concept of probability properly ought to belong to the domain of mathematics.

quote.translation: According to Laplace, "the ratio of the number of favourable cases to the number of all possible cases is the measure of probability, and probability is nothing other than a fraction whose numerator is the number of favourable cases and whose denominator is the number of all possible cases" (Laplace, Essai philosophique sur les Probabilités, Paris, Gauthier-Villars, 1921, p. 6).

quote.translation: In Cournot's formulation, probability is "the ratio of the number of chance occasions favourable to the event to the total number of chance occasions" (Cournot, l. c., p. 24).

quote.translation: Mises defines probability as follows: "The limiting value of the relative frequency with which a given mark appears (with the proviso that this limiting value must be insensitive to place selection) is called the probability of the appearance of this mark within the collective under consideration" (Richard von Mises, Wahrscheinlichkeit, Statistik und Wahrheit, 1928, S. 29).
